title: Nuclear Fusion
short_intro: Nuclear fusion is a nuclear reaction in which two or more atomic nuclei collide at very high speeds and combine to form a new type of atomic nucleus, releasing enormous amounts of energy. This process powers active stars and thermonuclear weapons.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of nuclear fusion, basic understanding of mass defect, energy release in proton-proton chain and carbon-nitrogen cycle, comparison with nuclear fission, and conditions required for fusion (high temperature and pressure).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed reaction cross-sections, Coulomb barrier penetration probability via quantum tunneling, Gamow peak derivation, Lawson criterion for controlled thermonuclear fusion, and magnetic/inertial confinement concepts.

prerequisites: Binding energy per nucleon curve and nuclear stability
Coulomb electrostatic repulsion between charged nuclei

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Mechanism of Nuclear Fusion
bullets: Light nuclei are brought within the range of the strong nuclear force (approx. 1 to 3 fm), overcoming their mutual electrostatic Coulomb repulsion.
The total rest mass of the product nuclei is less than the total rest mass of the reactant nuclei, yielding a positive mass defect (Δm).
The missing mass is converted directly into energy according to E = (Δm)c<sup>2</sup>, which appears as kinetic energy of the reaction products and gamma radiation.

concept_notes.heading: Stellar Fusion Cycles
bullets: In stars like the Sun, the primary energy source is the proton-proton (p-p) chain, converting four protons into one <sup>4</sup>He nucleus and two positrons, with a net energy release of about 26.7 MeV.
In heavier and hotter stars (T > 1.5 × 10<sup>7</sup> K), the Carbon-Nitrogen-Oxygen (CNO) cycle acts as a catalytic pathway for hydrogen fusion.
Deuterium-Tritium (D-T) fusion has the lowest ignition temperature and highest cross-section, making it the primary reaction studied for terrestrial controlled fusion reactors.

concept_notes.heading: The Coulomb Barrier and Quantum Tunneling
bullets: Two positively charged nuclei experience a strong Coulomb repulsive potential barrier V<sub>c</sub> = (1 / 4πε<sub>0</sub>) (q<sub>1</sub>q<sub>2</sub> / r), which is typically on the order of hundreds of kiloelectronvolts (keV).
Thermal energies in stellar cores (kT ~ 1 keV) are far lower than the classical Coulomb barrier height, meaning particles lack classical turning points to touch.
Fusion proceeds due to quantum mechanical wave-particle duality, allowing particles to tunnel through the Coulomb potential barrier with a finite transmission probability.

concept_notes.heading: Lawson Criterion for Controlled Fusion
bullets: The Lawson criterion specifies the minimum product of plasma density (n), confinement time (τ<sub>E</sub>), and plasma temperature (T) required for a fusion reactor to achieve ignition.
Ignition occurs when the power generated by alpha particles produced in fusion reactions equals or exceeds the total radiation and conduction losses.
For a D-T plasma, the required temperature is approximately 1 to 2 × 10<sup>8</sup> K (or 10 to 20 keV).

derivations.title: Energy Release (Q-value) in Deuterium-Tritium Fusion
steps: Write the mass balance equation using atomic mass units (u): m(<sup>2</sup>H) + m(<sup>3</sup>H) = m(<sup>4</sup>He) + m(n).
Substitute atomic masses: m(<sup>2</sup>H) = 2.014102 u, m(<sup>3</sup>H) = 3.016049 u, m(<sup>4</sup>He) = 4.001506 u, m(n) = 1.008665 u.
Calculate total initial mass: M<sub>i</sub> = 2.014102 + 3.016049 = 5.030151 u.
Calculate total final mass: M<sub>f</sub> = 4.001506 + 1.008665 = 5.010171 u.
Determine mass defect Δm = M<sub>i</sub> - M<sub>f</sub> = 5.030151 u - 5.010171 u = 0.019980 u.
Convert mass defect to energy using 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c<sup>2</sup>.

derivations.title: Gamow Peak Derivation Context for Reaction Rate
derivations.conditions: Maxwell-Boltzmann thermal distribution combined with quantum tunneling probability (Gamow factor)
steps: The Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution gives the relative number of particles with kinetic energy E as proportional to exp(-E / kT).
The quantum mechanical transmission coefficient (Gamow factor) for two nuclei with charges Z<sub>1</sub>e and Z<sub>2</sub>e is proportional to exp(-b / sqrt(E)), where b is the Gamow constant.
The total reaction rate is proportional to the product of these two competing functions: P(E) ∼ exp(-E / kT - b / sqrt(E)).
Differentiate the exponent with respect to E and set to zero to find the most probable energy (Gamow peak energy E<sub>0</sub>) at which nuclear reactions occur.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Binding Energy per Nucleon vs Mass Number Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of binding energy per nucleon (B.E./A) in MeV on the y-axis against mass number (A) on the x-axis, showing a sharp rise for light nuclei, a peak near A = 56 (Iron), and a slow decline for heavy nuclei.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Light nuclei (such as hydrogen, deuterium, helium) have low binding energy per nucleon. When they fuse to form heavier nuclei up to iron, the binding energy per nucleon increases, releasing the difference as binding energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in TGT/PGT to explain why fusion is exothermic for light nuclei and fission is exothermic for heavy nuclei.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fusion Reaction Cross-Section vs Energy
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A log-linear plot of nuclear fusion cross-section (σ) in barns versus center-of-mass energy (E) in keV, showing a steep rise from threshold and a distinct resonance peak (e.g., around 100 keV for D-T reaction) followed by a gradual decrease.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At very low energies, the Coulomb barrier suppresses the cross-section. As energy increases, quantum tunneling probability rises exponentially until thermal motion and nuclear cross-section peak.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT to explain optimal operating temperatures for thermonuclear reactors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann and Gamow Window Overlap
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two overlapping curves on an energy axis: a Maxwell-Boltzmann thermal distribution curve shifting downward with energy, and a steeply rising quantum penetration probability curve, whose product forms a distinct bell-shaped Gamow peak.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that fusion does not happen at the highest thermal energies or at zero energy, but within a narrow energy band (the Gamow window).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in PGT conceptual questions regarding stellar nucleosynthesis rates.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the energy released in the fusion of two deuterium nuclei to form a helium-3 nucleus and a neutron: <sup>2</sup>H + <sup>2</sup>H → <sup>3</sup>He + n. Given masses: m(<sup>2</sup>H) = 2.014102 u, m(<sup>3</sup>He) = 3.016029 u, m(n) = 1.008665 u. (Take 1 u = 931.5 MeV)
solution_steps: Find total mass of reactants: M<sub>i</sub> = 2 × 2.014102 u = 4.028204 u.
Find total mass of products: M<sub>f</sub> = 3.016029 u + 1.008665 u = 4.024694 u.
Calculate mass defect Δm = M<sub>i</sub> - M<sub>f</sub> = 4.028204 u - 4.024694 u = 0.003510 u.
Calculate energy released Q = 0.003510 u × 931.5 MeV/u.

solved_numericals.question: Estimate the height of the Coulomb potential barrier (in MeV) between two protons when their centers are separated by a distance equal to the sum of their nuclear radii, assuming R = 1.2 × 10<sup>-15</sup> A<sup>1/3</sup> m with A = 1 for a proton.
solution_steps: Determine the closest separation distance r = 2R = 2 × 1.2 × 10<sup>-15</sup> m = 2.4 × 10<sup>-15</sup> m.
Write Coulomb barrier formula: V<sub>c</sub> = (1 / 4πε<sub>0</sub>) × (e<sup>2</sup> / r).
Substitute constants: (1 / 4πε<sub>0</sub>) = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> C<sup>-2</sup>, e = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C.
Convert to MeV by dividing by 1.6 × 10<sup>-13</sup> J/MeV.

solved_numericals.question: A thermonuclear reactor operates on D-T fusion releasing 17.6 MeV per reaction. If the reactor generates a thermal power of 500 MW, find the number of deuterium nuclei consumed per second.
solution_steps: Energy per reaction in Joules: E = 17.6 MeV = 17.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> × 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> J = 2.816 × 10<sup>-12</sup> J.
Number of reactions per second n = P / E = (500 × 10<sup>6</sup>) / (2.816 × 10<sup>-12</sup>).
Since each D-T reaction consumes exactly one deuterium nucleus, the rate of deuterium consumption equals n.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution holds true for core stellar plasmas; limitation: high-energy tails can deviate in non-equilibrium plasmas.
Assumption: Quantum tunneling can be modeled using static Coulomb potentials; limitation: screening effects from surrounding electrons alter the effective barrier in dense laboratory plasmas.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Nuclear fusion only releases energy for hydrogen isotopes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Fusion is exothermic for any light nuclei up to iron (A = 56). Beyond iron, fusion absorbs energy.
common_misconceptions.why: The binding energy per nucleon curve peaks at iron; combining nuclei lighter than iron increases binding energy and releases excess mass energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Particles in a star collide with sufficient thermal energy to overcome the Coulomb barrier classically.
common_misconceptions.correct: Thermal energies in stellar cores are ~1 keV, whereas the Coulomb barrier is ~1 MeV.
common_misconceptions.why: Fusion occurs primarily due to quantum mechanical tunneling through the potential barrier at energies well below the classical threshold.

quick_revision: Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy due to mass defect.
The proton-proton chain powers standard stars, while the CNO cycle operates in massive stars.
Quantum tunneling is essential for fusion because thermal energies are much lower than Coulomb barrier heights.
D-T fusion yields 17.6 MeV and has the lowest ignition threshold for terrestrial reactors.
The Lawson criterion sets the required density, temperature, and confinement time for sustained fusion energy.
